sections.title: Global Equities
sections.content:
June 2026 delivered a mixed global equity tape, with U.S. benchmarks posting their first monthly decline after back-to-back gains in April and May, even as divergent forces — a historic oil-price collapse following the U.S.–Iran peace framework, a hawkish Federal Reserve surprise under Chair Kevin Warsh, and a record wave of equity issuance headlined by the SpaceX IPO — pulled markets in competing directions. The S&P 500 ended the month near **7,483**, down **-1%**, while the Dow Jones Industrial Average crossed the **52,000** threshold for the first time in its 130-year history on June 29 before settling at **52,305.24**; the Nasdaq Composite closed at **26,040.03**. Despite June's softness, H1 2026 performance remained exceptional: S&P **+9.6%**, Nasdaq **+12.8%**, Dow **+8.9%**.

European indices gave back ground across the board: the DAX shed **-2.76%**, the CAC 40 lost **-1.99%**, and the FTSE 100 fell **-1.70%**, all pressured by dollar strength, residual rate-tightening expectations, and energy-sector earnings downgrades. APAC delivered a bifurcated outcome — the Nikkei 225 touched an intra-month all-time high of **72,354** on AI and semiconductor enthusiasm before closing June at **70,062.32**, while the Hang Seng slipped **-0.6%** to **22,881.02** and the Shanghai Composite edged **+0.5%** to **4,094.40**.

The month's twin macro anchors — the resolution of the U.S.–Iran conflict, which sent Brent crude below **$80/bbl** and relieved stagflationary pressure, and the Warsh Fed's hawkish policy pivot, which tightened financial conditions via higher real yields and a surging dollar — shaped cross-asset returns in ways that rewarded selectivity over passive concentration. Broadening within equities, with value, healthcare, and cyclicals outperforming growth, suggests a potential inflection point in a rally that had been heavily concentrated in mega-cap technology.

sections.title: Your Must-Know Market Themes
sections.content: Four key themes that shaped markets this month:
themes:
SpaceX IPO & Record Half-Year Equity Issuance -- The singular capital markets event of June 2026 was the June 12 listing of SpaceX (ticker: SPCX), the largest initial public offering in history, raising **$86 billion** at an IPO price of **$135** per share and implying a valuation of **$1.77 trillion** at listing. SPCX surged to an intraday peak of **$225.64** on June 16 before settling near **$153** by late June — still a meaningful **+13%** premium to the issue price — and the debut briefly made Elon Musk the world's first U.S. dollar trillionaire by market capitalization.

The SpaceX listing was not isolated but the headline event in an extraordinary first-half for equity capital markets: Alphabet concurrently raised **$85 billion** in a landmark secondary equity offering, and total U.S. IPO and secondary issuance topped **$250 billion** for H1 2026 — a new half-year record. The depth of institutional and retail absorption of this historic supply without material index-level disruption underscored the extraordinary risk appetite and liquidity that characterized the 2026 bull market.

For portfolio allocators, the SpaceX IPO introduces a formidable new competitor for capital within the technology and aerospace theme. With several additional large-cap unicorns reportedly preparing H2 filings, the net supply of public equity is likely to accelerate further — a dynamic that strategists must factor into H2 positioning alongside an already elevated valuations environment.

US-Iran Peace Framework & Crude Oil Supply Shock Reversal -- The most disruptive commodity market dislocation in a generation began to reverse in June, as Washington and Tehran reached a framework ceasefire agreement reopening the Strait of Hormuz — a waterway handling 20% of global crude supply — to all international shipping. The IEA had estimated the Strait's closure was creating a daily global shortfall of **14 million barrels**, a supply shock without modern precedent that had driven WTI crude prices more than **40%** higher since the war's onset.

Brent crude fell **-5%** to **$78.96/bbl** on the day of the ceasefire announcement — the first sub-**$80** print since March — and continued lower toward approximately **$75/bbl** by month-end, as Iran's oil sanctions relief was structured to take effect immediately upon signing. Goldman Sachs subsequently cut its Q4 2026 Brent forecast to **$80/bbl** from a prior **$90/bbl**, reflecting expectations that Iranian barrels would gradually re-enter the global supply pool.

For equities, the deal was a material tailwind, reducing the stagflationary impulse that had weighed on risk assets and easing corporate input-cost pressures. The implications for energy-sector earnings in H2 2026, however, are considerably more challenging: E&P companies now navigate a structurally lower commodity price than consensus had assumed just weeks earlier, and 2026 guidance revisions are likely to be a source of earnings drag through the second half of the year.

Warsh's Hawkish Fed Pivot Reshapes the U.S. Rates Outlook -- Kevin Warsh's inaugural FOMC meeting as Federal Reserve Chair delivered a hawkish shock that upended the consensus that assumed a Trump-backed central banker would tilt dovish. The committee held the policy rate steady at **3.50%–3.75%** but removed key forward-guidance language signaling a future easing bias; nine of 18 FOMC participants now project at least one rate hike before year-end 2026, with six projecting two or more — a remarkable reversal of the dovish pivot markets had been pricing in.

The reaction was swift and severe: the 2-year Treasury yield surged more than **16 basis points** on the announcement day — the largest single-session move on a Fed decision day since March 2008 — while the U.S. dollar accelerated, with the DXY gaining **+2.3%** for the month to a 13-month high near **101.8**. USD/JPY climbed toward **160.85** — its highest level since July 2024 — raising the probability of Japanese Ministry of Finance intervention and triggering a significant unwind in yen-funded carry trades.

The macro implications are far-reaching: a rate-hike cycle restart — the first since 2022–2023 — was not discounted by equity or credit markets entering June. The resulting repricing of the risk-free rate has introduced meaningful uncertainty into H2 2026 earnings multiple assumptions, with rate-sensitive sectors including real estate, utilities, and long-duration growth equities facing incremental headwinds, while the banking sector stands to benefit from wider net interest margins if the hiking cycle materializes.

Alphabet Joins the Dow & The Broadening of Market Leadership -- On June 29, Alphabet (GOOGL) replaced Verizon Communications in the Dow Jones Industrial Average — the most significant index reconstitution in years — with S&P Dow Jones Indices citing Alphabet's enhanced exposure to artificial intelligence, cloud infrastructure, and digital advertising as the rationale for adding the name at the expense of a telecom holding. Alphabet shares rose **+3.7%** to **$350.24** on debut day, and the Dow crossed **52,000** for the first time in its 130-year history, closing at **52,120** on June 29 before settling at **52,305.24** at month-end.

Beyond the index optics, June saw a meaningful and potentially durable rotation in market leadership. Value beat growth, healthcare posted its best monthly performance since November, industrials and financials outperformed, and equal-weight benchmarks significantly outpaced their cap-weighted counterparts — precisely the broadening that portfolio strategists have characterized as necessary for a sustainable multi-year bull market. The U.S. flash composite PMI rose to **52.2** in June, with the manufacturing sub-index climbing to **55.7** — its highest reading since May 2022 — providing fundamental validation for the cyclical rotation narrative.

If the broadening beyond mega-cap technology that emerged in June is sustained through Q3 and Q4, it would represent a critical evolution of the current bull market: from a narrow, AI-concentration-driven advance into a broad-based expansion of earnings growth. This scenario has material implications for active management alpha, sector allocation, and the relative attractiveness of mid- and small-cap equities versus the mega-cap names that have dominated since 2024.

sections.title: US Equities
sections.content:
U.S. equity markets posted a measured setback in June, with the S&P 500 declining **-1%** to close near **7,483** — its first losing month after back-to-back gains of **+10.5%** in April and **+5.3%** in May. The retreat was orderly rather than disorderly, driven primarily by a hawkish repricing of the Federal Reserve's policy trajectory following Chair Warsh's inaugural FOMC meeting, which compressed multiples in rate-sensitive and longer-duration growth equities while pushing Treasury yields and the dollar higher. Despite June's softness, H1 2026 performance remained exceptional, with the S&P up **+9.6%** and the Nasdaq up **+12.8%** for the half-year.

The Nasdaq Composite closed at **26,040.03**, with semiconductor names coming under notable pressure through the back half of the month after their extraordinary prior-month run; the Nasdaq had posted at least five losing sessions in the final two weeks of June. The Dow Jones Industrial Average was the relative standout, closing at **52,305.24** — a new record — powered by the landmark addition of Alphabet on June 29 as a member of the blue-chip index. Alphabet's debut on the Dow pushed the index above **52,000** for the first time in its history, with Alphabet shares rallying **+3.7%** to **$350.24** on the day.

Beneath the headline indices, June's most consequential development was the broadening of market leadership. Healthcare posted its best monthly performance since November; financials and industrials outperformed; equal-weight benchmarks significantly outpaced cap-weighted equivalents; and value trounced growth. The month also set a new record for U.S. equity issuance — anchored by SpaceX's **$86 billion** IPO on June 12, the largest in history — with total H1 2026 IPO and secondary sales topping **$250 billion**, a half-year record that signals both exceptional corporate confidence and deep market liquidity.

sections.title: European Equities
sections.content:
European equity markets surrendered ground across the board in June, with the DAX declining **-2.76%**, the CAC 40 losing **-1.99%**, and the FTSE 100 falling **-1.70%**, all three indices pressured by a combination of dollar strength, resurgent ECB rate-tightening expectations, and the structural disadvantage of a region with limited AI and semiconductor exposure relative to the U.S. and Japan. The ECB's June 11 decision — which held rates while signaling a more cautious posture on future easing — reinforced concerns that European monetary conditions would remain tighter for longer, compressing credit availability and dampening corporate capital deployment.

The collapse in crude oil prices following the U.S.-Iran peace framework offered a partial offset for energy-importing European economies, with airlines, logistics, and consumer discretionary names catching a bid on lower input-cost expectations. However, FTSE 100 energy producers — including several major North Sea operators — gave back significant ground as Brent fell toward **$75/bbl**, threatening fiscal break-evens and dividend coverage ratios in energy names that had been key index constituents. The eurozone composite PMI remained above 50, suggesting ongoing expansion, but the narrative was overshadowed by dollar-strength headwinds and the potential ripple effects of the Warsh Fed's hawkish pivot on global financial conditions.

The relative underperformance of European equities versus the U.S. in June extends a year-to-date pattern of episodic compression in European risk premiums. With the ECB holding and the Fed now signaling potential hikes, the rate-differential dynamic is shifting in ways that may attract incremental capital toward dollar-denominated assets at the expense of European ones. Investors will be watching Q2 earnings season closely for signs that European corporate margins can absorb higher financing costs and weaker Chinese demand — two of the defining challenges facing the region's export-oriented economy heading into H2 2026.

sections.title: APAC Equities
sections.content:
Asia-Pacific equity markets delivered a sharply bifurcated outcome in June, with Japan's Nikkei 225 surging to fresh all-time highs on continued artificial intelligence and semiconductor investment tailwinds, while Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index underperformed materially, closing the month at **22,881.02** — down **-0.6%** — weighed by softer consumer internet sentiment and persistent uncertainty about Chinese domestic demand. The divergence between Tokyo's strength and Hong Kong's weakness crystallized the defining regional investment theme of 2026: a decisive global preference for AI infrastructure and semiconductor exposure over traditional consumer internet platforms.

The Nikkei 225 was the standout, touching an intra-month all-time high of **72,354** driven by enthusiasm around AI and semiconductor manufacturing, before paring gains to close June at **70,062.32**. The advance reflected structural enthusiasm for Japan's semiconductor supply-chain buildout, yen-weakness-driven earnings tailwinds for exporters, and sustained foreign institutional inflows into Japanese equities as a global AI-capex proxy. South Korea's KOSPI similarly outperformed the broader APAC region on its semiconductor exposure, while China's Shanghai Composite posted a modest **+0.5%** advance to close at **4,094.40**, with gains concentrated in a single catch-up session following the Dragon Boat Festival holiday.

Structurally, China's equity market continues to trade in a constrained range, with policymakers balancing targeted demand-side stimulus against persistent property-sector headwinds and geopolitical trade uncertainty. The People's Bank of China held policy rates steady through June, keeping its powder dry as it assessed the impact of the U.S.-Iran resolution on global commodity prices and trade flows. For APAC allocators, the key question entering H2 2026 is whether Chinese policy stimulus will be sufficient to close the performance gap with the region's AI-driven outperformers, or whether the Nikkei versus Hang Seng divergence will widen further.

sections.title: Foreign Exchange
sections.content:
The U.S. dollar dominated the June FX tape, with the DXY index advancing **+2.3%** to close near **101.8** — a 13-month high — building on May's **+0.9%** gain and marking the broadest G10 dollar advance since early 2025. The primary catalyst was the hawkish pivot from the Warsh-led Federal Reserve, which widened the U.S. rate differential decisively in the dollar's favor: the 2-year Treasury yield advanced **+17 basis points** over the month, while yields in the eurozone, UK, and Japan either held steady or declined, amplifying the carry advantage of long-USD positions.

EUR/USD fell from **1.1683** at end-May to **1.1422** at June month-end — a decline of **-2.2%** — as ECB rate-hike expectations faded and eurozone growth signals remained uneven. GBP/USD held relatively better, settling near **1.34**, supported by sticky UK services inflation and Bank of England pricing that kept residual hike probabilities alive. USD/JPY was the focal cross of the month, surging to **160.85** — its highest level since July 2024 — as the Bank of Japan maintained its ultra-accommodative stance against the backdrop of rising U.S. yields, pushing the pair toward the threshold that previously triggered Ministry of Finance intervention.

The broader FX takeaway from June is a decisive re-rating of U.S. monetary exceptionalism under Chair Warsh. Markets that entered the month pricing in an eventual easing pivot found themselves wrong-footed, with the hawkish recalibration repricing the dollar sharply higher across the board. The strategic risk entering H2 2026 is twofold: the potential for disorderly yen depreciation that forces Japanese authorities to intervene — disrupting global carry-trade dynamics — and an emerging-market FX channel where a stronger dollar tightens financial conditions for dollar-denominated borrowers across Asia and Latin America.

sections.title: Commodities
sections.content:
Crude oil was the defining commodity story of June, with Brent and WTI posting sharp month-on-month declines following the U.S.–Iran framework peace agreement. Brent — which had surged more than **40%** since the outbreak of the conflict due to the Strait of Hormuz closure (the IEA estimated a daily global supply shortfall of **14 million barrels**) — fell **-5%** to **$78.96/bbl** on the day of the ceasefire announcement and continued lower to **$75/bbl** by month-end, as Iran's oil sanctions relief was structured to take effect immediately upon signing. Goldman Sachs subsequently cut its Q4 2026 Brent forecast to **$80/bbl** from a prior **$90/bbl**, reflecting expectations that Iranian barrels would gradually re-enter the global supply pool.

Gold retreated from its earlier highs above **$4,500/oz**, settling near **$4,320/oz** by mid-June as the safe-haven bid unwound alongside reduced geopolitical risk premium from the Iran deal, and rising real U.S. yields — a byproduct of the Warsh Fed's hawkish pivot — capped the metal's upside. Structurally, central bank demand and residual geopolitical uncertainty continue to provide a floor, but the near-term risk-reward for gold shifted less favorable as the Iran crisis discount unwound and dollar strength created an additional headwind for the non-yielding metal.

Copper was the notable outperformer across the commodity complex, surging **+6%** month-on-month to close near **$6.39/lb** — approaching its all-time high of **$6.67/lb** reached intra-month — driven by robust Chinese import volumes, rising speculative long positioning, and structural supply constraints in the global copper mining pipeline. The divergence between falling crude and rising copper captures a key commodity market message: the energy supply shock was idiosyncratic and resolvable, while the structural demand for industrial metals tied to electrification and AI infrastructure buildout remains intact and demand-inelastic.

sections.title: Fixed Income
sections.content:
U.S. Treasury markets experienced one of their most consequential single-meeting repricings in years in June, as the Warsh-led Federal Reserve's inaugural FOMC meeting delivered a hawkish shock that sent the 2-year Treasury yield surging more than **16 basis points** on the announcement day — the largest single-session move on a Fed decision day since March 2008. The Fed held the federal funds rate steady at **3.50%–3.75%** but removed key policy-statement language signaling a future easing bias; nine of 18 FOMC members now project at least one rate hike before year-end 2026, with six projecting two or more — a dot-plot configuration that was materially more hawkish than pre-meeting market pricing.

The 10-year Treasury yield settled near **4.38%** by late June, while the 2-year yield reached **4.07%**, maintaining a positively sloped yield curve with a spread of **+31 basis points**. The positive curve slope, while modest, marked a meaningful contrast to the deeply inverted readings that defined the 2023–2024 period and represents a tentative normalization of the term structure, though the near-term risk is that further hawkish signaling re-inverts the curve if short-end yields reprice more aggressively than the long end.

Corporate bonds remained broadly resilient despite the rates shock, with investment-grade spreads holding contained even as high-yield saw modest widening in credit-sensitive sectors. Global sovereign bonds outside the U.S. posted modest gains as yields in the eurozone, UK, and Japan held steady or declined — a divergence that amplified dollar strength and set up a more complex global rates landscape heading into H2 2026. With nine FOMC members now projecting hikes, fixed income volatility is likely to remain elevated, and duration positioning represents a key risk factor for cross-asset portfolios entering the second half of the year.
